items.title: Google ships Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth new Gemini model in a month
items.summary: Google released Gemini 4 Neon, a new frontier model built for software development, knowledge work, and science. It handles text, images, video, audio, and PDFs with a context window of one million tokens. At $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, Neon is priced above previous Gemini 4 models. The article Google ships Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth new Gemini model in a month appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: Google Deepmind's Project Genie update brings Genie 4, chainable worlds, and a community gallery for remixing
items.summary: With Genie 4, Google DeepMind is launching its most realistic world model to date for Google AI Ultra subscribers. It generates interactive 3D worlds that can be modified in real time via text input and, for the first time, includes native sound. A community gallery allows users to share and remix the worlds they've created. items.title: Microsoft is replacing outside AI models in its own products with cheaper in-house alternatives
items.summary: Microsoft's AI division MAI unveiled seven new models for code, security, images, language, and routing at Ignite. MAI Code 2 reaches 98 percent of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40 percent of the cost, according to Microsoft. The models are built for running AI agents around the clock in enterprises. items.title: OpenAI says its models delivered a year's worth of chip optimization on top of AMD's own engineering
items.summary: Working with AMD, OpenAI achieved up to 14 percent PPA improvement on AMD's flagship GPU IP in less than five months. According to OpenAI, that's roughly a year's worth of progress, and AMD has already folded the changes into a design sent to production. Anthropic is also applying AI to chip work to optimize cost and performance per dollar. The article OpenAI says its models delivered a year's worth of chip optimization on top of AMD's own engine

items.title: Pangram flags 99 percent of an award-winning Peruvian novel as AI-generated, but the publisher stands by its author
items.summary: The AI detection tool Pangram flags 99 percent of a prize-winning Peruvian novel as AI-generated, but Mexican publisher Almadía is standing by the award after its own review. Pangram also classified over 80 percent of the author's personal texts as machine-written. French publisher Gallimard plans to start screening manuscripts with the tool. items.title: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models readily marked medics, journalists, and surrendering soldiers as kamikaze drone targets
items.summary: A Vals AI investigation shows that leading AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have almost no safeguards against use in autonomous weapons systems. In tests, the models readily flagged civilians as military targets, and a simple video game framing in the prompt was enough to override even belated refusals. The providers have promised fixes. items.title: OpenAI opens its AI systems to four independent on-site auditors for the first time
items.summary: OpenAI is giving four independent audit organizations, including Apollo Research and METR, direct access to unreleased models, source code, and training data for the first time. The embedded reviews are designed to uncover hidden misbehavior and safety gaps. items.title: Hugging Face now routes model requests through OpenRouter for the best price or speed
items.summary: Hugging Face now routes language model requests through OpenRouter, which automatically selects the cheapest or fastest provider. Bring-your-own API keys for language models are going away. According to OpenRouter, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46 percent. Both partners face multibillion-dollar acquisitions. The article Hugging Face now routes model requests through OpenRouter for the best price or speed appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: More than half the electricity feeding America's largest data centers comes from gas and coal
items.summary: A Harvard study published in Nature Sustainability found that 403 US hyperscale data centers produced roughly 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 between May 2024 and April 2025, more than all of Denmark. Over half of their electricity came from fossil fuels. With 2,000 additional facilities planned, the researchers warn of a major climate setback.
